novice.prompt: Which principle describes how a stack removes elements?
options: Last in, first out
First in, first out
Smallest value first
Random order
rubric: A stack removes the most recently added element first (LIFO).
First in, first out describes a queue.

novice.prompt: Which principle describes how a queue removes elements?
options: First in, first out
Last in, first out
Largest value first
Alphabetical order
rubric: A queue serves the oldest element first (FIFO).
Last in, first out describes a stack.

novice.prompt: What does a hash table use to decide where to store a key?
options: A hash function
A sorting routine
A linked list head
A binary search
rubric: A hash function maps the key to a bucket index.
Sorting and binary search belong to ordered structures, not hash tables.

novice.prompt: In a singly linked list, what does each node store besides its data?
options: A reference to the next node
A reference to the array index
The size of the list
A hash of the data
rubric: Each node holds data plus a pointer to the next node.
Size and index are not stored per node.

novice.prompt: What is the name of the top node of a tree, which has no parent?
options: Root
Leaf
Edge
Child
rubric: The root is the single node without a parent.
A leaf is a node with no children.

novice.prompt: Which of the following are standard operations of a stack? Select all that apply.
options: push
pop
enqueue
peek
dequeue
rubric: Push, pop and peek are stack operations.
Enqueue and dequeue belong to queues.

novice.prompt: A student reads that a min-heap is a tree where every parent is no larger than its children. They want to know which element can always be found at the root of such a heap. Which element is it?
options: The smallest element
The largest element
The median element
The most recently inserted element
rubric: In a min-heap the root holds the minimum.
The largest is the root of a max-heap.

novice.prompt: Why is reading `arr[5]` from an array fast regardless of array size?
options: The address is computed directly from the index
The array is scanned from the start
The elements are kept sorted
The index is looked up in a hash table
rubric: Contiguous memory lets the address be computed as base plus offset.
Scanning would make access slower for larger arrays.

novice.prompt: Why is inserting at the front of a linked list cheaper than at the front of an array?
options: No other elements need shifting, only a pointer changes
The list stores elements contiguously in memory
The list sorts its elements automatically
The array must be copied to disk first
rubric: Linked list insertion at the head only updates a reference.
Arrays must shift every element; lists are not contiguous.

novice.prompt: A browser's Back button returns to the previous page, then the one before it. Which structure fits this behaviour?
options: Stack
Queue
Hash table
Heap
rubric: Most recent page is revisited first, which is LIFO.
A queue would return the oldest page first.

novice.prompt: A print server must print documents in the order they were submitted. Which structure matches this?
options: Queue
Stack
Binary tree
Graph
rubric: Fair ordering by arrival is FIFO.
A stack would print the newest job first.

novice.prompt: What is a collision in a hash table?
options: Two different keys map to the same bucket
A key is stored twice in one bucket
The table runs out of memory
A key has no value assigned
rubric: Collisions occur when different keys hash to the same index.
Duplicate storage and memory exhaustion are different issues.

novice.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a graph? Select all that apply.
options: It consists of vertices connected by edges
It can model roads between cities
It must always have exactly one root
It can contain cycles
rubric: Graphs have vertices and edges, model networks, and may have cycles.
Having exactly one root is a tree property, not a graph one.

novice.prompt: A programmer stores 1,000 usernames and must frequently check whether a given name already exists. They consider an unsorted array or a hash table. Which choice is better and why?
options: Hash table, since lookup takes about constant time on average
Array, since lookup uses direct index access by name
Array, since it checks every name only once in constant time
Hash table, since it keeps names in alphabetical order
rubric: Hash tables give average constant-time membership checks; arrays need a full scan.
Index access works by position, not by name, and hash tables are not ordered.

expert.prompt: An open-addressing hash table with linear probing sees constant inserts and deletes. A teammate proposes deleting a key by simply marking its slot empty. Judge this against the criterion that every present key must stay findable.
options: Sound: an emptied slot frees space at once and lets later lookups stop sooner, which keeps probe sequences short
Flawed: an emptied slot ends probe chains early, so keys stored past it become unreachable; use tombstones or backward-shift deletion
Flawed: emptied slots corrupt the load factor count, so the whole table must be rehashed after every single delete
Sound: linear probing keeps colliding keys adjacent, so any key can be found by scanning on from its home slot
rubric: An empty slot is the stop signal for lookups, so emptying a mid-chain slot hides later keys; tombstones or backward shift preserve chains.
Distractors assume probing ignores empty slots or that deletes force rehashing.

expert.prompt: A reviewer says bottom-up heap construction is Theta(n log n) because it runs sift-down on about n/2 nodes, each costing O(log n). Which judgement of this claim is correct?
options: The claim holds: n/2 sift-downs at log n each is a tight bound, and the sum cannot be any lower
The claim is wrong: sift-down cost is bounded by node height and most nodes have small height, so the total sums to O(n)
The claim is wrong: bottom-up construction sorts the array first, so it costs O(n) comparisons using counting sort
The claim is wrong: sift-down on internal nodes costs O(1) regardless of their height, so the total is O(n)
rubric: Cost per node is proportional to its height; about n/2^(h+1) nodes have height h, and the sum of h/2^h converges, giving O(n).
Distractors multiply a worst case by a count or invent a constant-time sift-down.

expert.prompt: You must index 1 billion keys on disk. Each node access costs one 4 KB page read, and the criterion is to minimise page reads per lookup. Which structure is the best choice?
options: B-tree with fanout in the hundreds, since its height is about log base fanout of n, needing only a few page reads
Red-black tree, since its height is at most 2 log2 n and that worst-case guarantee keeps page reads low enough
AVL tree, since stricter balancing gives the lowest height of any binary tree and so the fewest page reads
Sorted array with binary search, since contiguous storage means each probe lands on a page already read
rubric: High fanout makes the tree shallow, so a lookup touches about 4 pages versus around 30 for any binary tree.
Distractors optimise binary-tree height or cache locality, ignoring the page-read cost.

expert.prompt: A dynamic array grows by a fixed 1000 slots each time it fills, copying all elements. A teammate says this is as good as doubling. Judge this against the criterion of total cost for n appends with very large n.
options: The claim holds: each resize copies only a bounded chunk, so appends stay amortized O(1) in either scheme
The claim is wrong: fixed growth gives about n^2/1000 copying in total, so appends are amortized O(n); geometric growth restores O(1)
The claim is wrong: doubling wastes up to half the memory, which makes its appends amortized O(log n) overall
The claim holds: in both schemes resizes happen less often than ordinary appends, so the cost per append is constant
rubric: With additive growth there are n/1000 resizes, each copying O(n), so total cost is quadratic; doubling makes copies sum to O(n).
Distractors confuse rarity of resizes with bounded cost, or misattribute a log factor to doubling.

expert.prompt: A graph has 50,000 vertices and about 1.2 billion edges. The workload is dominated by edge-existence queries, and the memory budget is 2 GB. Which representation best meets these criteria?
options: Adjacency lists of 32-bit ints, because storage scales with the edge count and iteration skips absent edges
Bit-packed adjacency matrix, because it takes about 300 MB and answers each edge test in constant time
Edge list sorted by source, because binary search answers edge queries and it needs the least memory
Hash set of edge pairs, because it gives constant expected lookups and uses less memory than a matrix
rubric: 50,000^2 bits is about 312 MB, well inside budget, with O(1) tests; the graph is dense enough that lists need several GB.
Distractors apply the sparse-graph rule of thumb or ignore per-entry overhead.

expert.prompt: Compare a skip list with a balanced binary search tree for an ordered in-memory map. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Search, insert and delete take expected O(log n) time, with the bound depending on random level choices
Worst-case O(log n) is guaranteed for every operation regardless of the random choices made
Range scans are simple: locate the start key, then walk the bottom-level list in order
Insertion needs no rotations, which makes lock-free concurrent variants easier than for balanced trees
rubric: Skip lists give expected, not worst-case, logarithmic bounds; they have an ordered bottom list and local pointer updates without rotations.
The worst-case guarantee option confuses probabilistic with deterministic balancing.

expert.prompt: A team runs Dijkstra on a sparse road graph with V vertices and E edges. Their library's binary heap has no decrease-key, so a colleague proposes pushing a new (distance, vertex) entry on every relaxation and skipping stale entries when popped. Judge this against the criterion of keeping the usual asymptotic cost.
options: Unsafe: duplicates can make the heap hold E entries, so each operation costs O(E) and the total becomes O(E^2)
Unsafe: skipping stale entries can discard a vertex's correct distance, so the shortest paths may come out wrong
Acceptable: the heap holds at most E entries and log E is at most 2 log V, so the total stays O((V+E) log V)
Acceptable only if the graph is a tree, because otherwise duplicate entries break the monotone order of pops
rubric: Lazy deletion bounds heap size by E, and log E = O(log V) since E < V^2, so the complexity matches the decrease-key version.
Distractors treat heap size as linear cost per operation or think stale entries corrupt correctness.

expert.prompt: Design a structure supporting insert, delete and getRandom (uniform over current items), each in expected O(1) time. Which design meets every constraint?
options: Dynamic array of items plus a hash map from item to index; on delete, swap with the last element, update the map, then pop
Hash map only; getRandom picks a random bucket and returns the first item found in it, which is uniform enough
Balanced BST; getRandom picks a random rank and walks down the tree using subtree sizes for all three operations
Doubly linked list plus a hash map to nodes; getRandom jumps to a node at a random list position by index
rubric: Swap-with-last keeps the array dense, giving O(1) deletion and uniform random access.
The BST costs O(log n); bucket sampling is non-uniform; a linked list cannot index in O(1).

expert.prompt: Design an algorithm that outputs the maximum of every window of size k over an array of n numbers in O(n) total time. Which design meets this?
options: Max-heap of window values; remove the outgoing element by scanning the heap at each step
Deque of indices kept in decreasing value order; pop smaller values from the back on arrival, pop the front when it leaves the window
Balanced BST of window values; read the maximum in O(log n) after each insertion and deletion
Array of window values, with a cached max that is recomputed only when the outgoing element equals it
rubric: Each index enters and leaves the deque once, giving O(n) total, with the front always holding the window maximum.
Other options cost O(k) or O(log k) per step, or degrade when the max keeps leaving.

expert.prompt: Design a FIFO queue supporting enqueue, dequeue and getMax, all in amortized O(1) time, using only stacks as building blocks. Which design works?
options: Two stacks (in and out), each storing pairs of value and max so far; move in to out when out is empty; max is the larger of the two tops
One queue plus a single variable for the max, recomputed by scanning only when the dequeued item was the max
Two stacks where only the in-stack tracks its max; after a transfer, the out-stack max is found by scanning it
A max-heap alongside the queue; dequeue removes the matching value from the heap in constant time
rubric: Each stack tracks a running max, so the queue max is the larger of two O(1) reads; transfers are amortized O(1).
The other options need O(n) scans or O(log n) heap deletion.

expert.prompt: A server stores user-supplied strings in a hash table. An attacker crafts many keys that collide, degrading lookups to O(n). Which fix meets all constraints: expected O(1) lookups even against a known algorithm, and no per-key extra structures?
options: Double the table size at startup so fewer keys collide on any input the attacker chooses
Use a keyed hash with a secret random seed chosen per process, so collisions cannot be predicted in advance
Switch to a fixed, stronger-looking mixing function, so finding colliding keys needs too much computation
Keep each bucket as a sorted array and binary-search it, which gives O(log n) lookups on any collision set
rubric: A secret random seed (universal or keyed hashing) restores expected O(1) because attackers cannot precompute collisions.
A fixed function can be attacked offline, resizing doesn't stop crafted collisions, and sorted buckets lose O(1).

expert.prompt: Design a dynamic ordered set supporting insert, delete, rank(x) (count of items below x) and select(k) (the k-th smallest), each in O(log n) worst case. Which design meets all four?
options: Balanced BST where each node stores its subtree size, maintained on rotations; rank and select walk down comparing sizes
Sorted array with binary search for rank and direct indexing for select; inserts and deletes shift elements
Hash map of keys to counts plus a min-heap; select pops k items and pushes them back afterwards
Balanced BST keyed by value alone; select does an in-order traversal counting nodes until reaching position k
rubric: Augmenting a balanced BST with subtree sizes makes rank and select logarithmic while updates remain O(log n).
The array has O(n) updates; the heap and plain traversal make select linear or worse.

expert.prompt: A calendar service stores intervals in an array sorted by start time. It must support insert, delete and 'find any stored interval overlapping a query interval', each in O(log n). Which two changes make the design meet all constraints? Select all that apply.
options: Store intervals in a balanced BST keyed by start time instead of an array
In each node keep the maximum end time in its subtree, refreshed during rotations
Hash intervals by start time so an overlapping one is found by probing nearby keys
Keep a second array sorted by end time and binary-search it for the query start
rubric: A balanced BST gives O(log n) updates, and the subtree max-end lets a query prune branches that cannot overlap.
Hashing destroys order, and a sorted-by-end array still has O(n) updates and no pruning.

expert.prompt: A monitoring service receives a stream of latency readings and must report the running median after every reading. Constraints: each insert in O(log n), each median query in O(1), memory O(n), and no re-sorting of earlier data. Which design satisfies all constraints?
options: Keep a sorted array, inserting by binary search and shifting; the median is the middle element
Keep one min-heap of all values; find the median by popping half the elements and pushing them back
Keep a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, rebalanced so sizes differ by at most one
Keep a hash map of value counts and a running mean; report the mean as an approximation of the median
rubric: Two balanced heaps expose the median at their tops in O(1), with O(log n) insert and rebalancing.
The sorted array has O(n) inserts, the single heap makes queries O(n log n), and the mean is not the median.

competent.prompt: A min-heap is stored in a 0-indexed array as `[2, 5, 3, 9, 6]`. The value 1 is inserted using the standard append-then-sift-up procedure. What does the array contain afterwards?
rubric: 1 is appended at index 5, swaps with its parent 3 at index 2, then swaps with the root 2.
Distractors come from stopping after one swap, or swapping with the wrong parent index.

competent.prompt: A hash table has 7 buckets and uses chaining, with new nodes appended at the tail of a chain. The hash is `key % 7`. Keys 15, 22, 9 and 29 are inserted in that order. How many nodes are examined to find 29?
rubric: 15, 22 and 29 all hash to bucket 1, so the chain is 15, 22, 29 and finding 29 takes 3 examinations.
Choosing 1 assumes direct access, and choosing 4 counts the node for key 9 in another bucket.

competent.prompt: A stack-based evaluator processes the postfix expression `3 4 + 2 * 5 -` from left to right. What value is left on the stack at the end?
rubric: 14 comes from forgetting the final subtraction, and 1 from reversing the operand order for subtraction.

competent.prompt: Keys 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4 are inserted in that order into an initially empty binary search tree with no balancing. What is the preorder traversal (node, left, right)?
rubric: The tree has root 8, left subtree 3(1, 6(4)) and right subtree 10(14); preorder visits each node before its children.
1 3 4 6 8 10 14 is inorder, 8 3 10 1 6 14 4 is insertion order, and the last is postorder.

competent.prompt: A circular queue uses an array of capacity 5. It has `front = 3` and currently holds 4 elements. At which array index is the next enqueued element stored?
rubric: The next slot is (front + size) % capacity = (3 + 4) % 5 = 2.
The other indices are occupied slots (3, 4, 0, 1 hold the current elements) or forget the wrap-around.

competent.prompt: Which of the following operations run in constant time, either amortised or worst case, with the stated structure and information? Select all that apply.
options: Appending an element to the end of a dynamic array (amortised)
Inserting a new element at index 0 of an array holding n items
Reading the minimum value from a binary min-heap without removing it
Reading the k-th element of a singly linked list
Removing the first node of a singly linked list, given its head pointer
rubric: Append is amortised O(1), peeking at the heap root is O(1), and removing the head only changes one pointer.
Inserting at the front of an array shifts n items, and reaching the k-th linked-list node needs a walk of k steps.

competent.prompt: You are building a feature that shows the fewest connection hops between two users. The social graph is stored as an adjacency list and contains many cycles. You write a breadth-first search from the first user. Which frontier structure and bookkeeping give correct shortest hop counts without looping forever?
options: A stack, with a visited set so each user is expanded only once
A queue, with a visited set so each user is added at most once
A min-heap ordered by user id, so lower ids are expanded first
A queue with no visited set, since hop counts are tracked level by level
rubric: BFS needs a FIFO queue to process users by increasing hop distance, and a visited set to stop cycles from looping.
A stack gives depth-first order, which does not guarantee shortest hops, and omitting the visited set loops forever on cycles.

competent.prompt: A Python program processes one million tasks by repeatedly calling `tasks.pop(0)` on a list in a loop and takes far longer than expected. Which diagnosis best explains the slowdown?
options: Each `pop(0)` shifts every remaining element left, so each removal costs O(n) and the loop is O(n^2) overall
Each `pop(0)` reallocates the whole list, so memory use grows quadratically with the number of tasks left
Python lists are linked internally, so each removal from the front must walk the chain from the tail
Each `pop(0)` re-sorts the list to keep order, which costs O(n log n) on every call
rubric: A Python list is an array, so removing from the front moves all later elements, giving quadratic total work; a deque avoids this.
Distractors invent reallocation, linked internals or sorting that the operation does not do.

competent.prompt: A chained hash table has 1000 buckets and hashes integer keys with `key % 1000`. After loading keys such as 1000, 2000, 3000 and so on, lookups become linear in the number of entries. What is the cause?
options: The load factor exceeds 1, so the table must resize before any key can be placed in a bucket
Every key is a multiple of 1000, so all keys land in bucket 0 and form one long chain
Chaining always degrades to linear time once the table holds more than 1000 entries, whatever the hash
Keys this large overflow the hash function, which sends them to a few arbitrary buckets
rubric: Each multiple of 1000 has remainder 0, so the hash function and key pattern interact badly and everything collides in one bucket.
Other options blame load factor, chaining in general or overflow, but the problem is the poor key distribution.

competent.prompt: Appending n items to a dynamic array that grows by a fixed 10 slots when full costs O(n^2) in total, while doubling the capacity gives O(n). Which explanation is correct?
options: Fixed growth makes every individual append O(n) in the worst case, whereas doubling makes every append O(1)
Fixed growth cannot reuse old memory, so the allocator takes O(n) time to find space regardless of copying
Fixed growth causes about n/10 resizes that each copy all current elements, so total copying is quadratic
Fixed growth forces a resize on every append after size 10, because capacity never exceeds length plus 10
rubric: The number of resizes grows linearly with n and each copies a linear number of elements, giving quadratic total work; doubling makes copies sum to O(n).
The worst-case claim for doubling is false, since one doubling append still copies n items.

competent.prompt:
This code reverses a singly linked list:
`prev = None; curr = head`
`while curr:`
`    curr.next = prev`
`    prev = curr`
`    curr = curr.next`
`return prev`
What happens for the list 1 -> 2 -> 3?
options: It returns 3 -> 2 -> 1 because each link is flipped in turn
It returns only node 1, and nodes 2 and 3 are lost from the list
It loops forever because `curr.next` points back to a visited node
It raises an error on the first iteration because `prev` is `None`
rubric: After `curr.next = prev`, `curr.next` is `None`, so `curr` becomes `None` and the loop ends with only node 1; the next pointer must be saved first.
Learners who skim the code assume the standard reversal result or an infinite loop.

competent.prompt: A plain, unbalanced binary search tree is built by inserting keys read from an already sorted file. Lookups then grow linearly slower as keys are added. What is the cause?
options: Sorted input fills the left subtree first and leaves the right empty, so lookups scan about half the nodes
Sorted input balances the tree perfectly, but each node stores a parent pointer, so lookups need extra memory reads
Ascending inserts trigger repeated rotations to rebalance the tree, and the rotation cost dominates lookups
Each ascending key goes right of the previous one, producing a chain of height n, so lookups cost O(n)
rubric: Without balancing, ascending inserts make a right-leaning chain, which behaves like a linked list.
A plain BST has no rotations, and sorted input does not produce a balanced tree.

competent.prompt: A team wants to find every key between 100 and 200 in a large hash table and finds it very slow. Which statements correctly explain why? Select all that apply.
options: The hash function scatters adjacent keys across unrelated buckets, so keys in a range are not stored near each other
Bucket order carries no key ordering, so a range query must examine every bucket
Average single-key lookup is linear, which makes any query on a hash table slow
Hash tables can only hold fixed-size integer keys, which breaks the comparisons a range needs
rubric: Hashing destroys key order, so a range query has no starting point and must scan all buckets.
Average lookup is O(1), not linear, and hash tables are not limited to integer keys.

competent.prompt: A routing tool runs Dijkstra's algorithm on a road graph with 100,000 nodes and 300,000 edges stored as adjacency lists. The frontier is a plain unsorted array, and each step scans it for the closest unsettled node. Runs take minutes. What is the main cause?
options: Edge relaxation costs O(V) per edge on adjacency lists, so the 300,000 edges dominate; a matrix would be faster
Dijkstra needs a stack to backtrack along shortest paths, and an array-based stack is slow at this size
Each step scans the whole frontier for the minimum, giving about V^2 work, where a binary heap gives O((V+E) log V)
The array grows by doubling during the run, and those resizes dominate the cost on a graph this sparse
rubric: Scanning for the minimum is O(V) per extraction, giving roughly 10^10 operations; a heap makes extraction O(log V).
The other options misplace the cost in relaxation, backtracking or resizing, none of which dominates here.

proficient.prompt: A hash table with chaining and a fixed 16 buckets receives 1 million keys. Lookups were fast at 10,000 keys but now take far longer, growing roughly linearly with the key count. What is the most precise diagnosis?
options: The load factor grew unbounded, so chains lengthen in proportion to n and lookups degrade toward O(n/16)
The hash function must be producing collisions on every key, which no table size could fix at any scale
Chained buckets use linked lists, and list nodes cause cache misses that scale lookups with total memory
The table is too small to hold the keys, so inserts silently overwrite and lookups search the whole table
rubric: Without resizing, average chain length is n/buckets, so lookup cost grows linearly with n.
Distractors blame the hash function, cache effects or overwriting, none of which explains linear growth with a fixed bucket count.

proficient.prompt: A binary search tree is built by inserting 1, 2, 3, ..., 10000 in order, with no balancing. A search for key 10000 is very slow compared with a search in a tree built from the same keys inserted in random order. Why?
options: Sorted insertion makes every node a right child, so height is n and the search walks a linked-list-like path
Sorted insertion places large keys near the root, so the search must backtrack through many left subtrees
Random insertion yields a complete tree, so its height is exactly log2(n) and sorted insertion cannot match it
Duplicate comparisons occur on sorted input, so each node is visited twice and search cost doubles
rubric: Ascending inserts always go right, giving a degenerate tree of height n.
Random order gives expected O(log n) height but not a perfectly complete tree; the other options misdescribe BST behaviour.

proficient.prompt: A queue is implemented as a dynamic array where dequeue removes index 0 and shifts all remaining elements left. Enqueue is amortised O(1). A profile shows throughput collapsing when the queue holds about 100,000 items. Which analysis explains this?
options: Each dequeue costs O(n) because of the shift, so draining n items costs O(n^2) in total
Each enqueue triggers resizing, so the amortised O(1) bound fails once the array grows past a certain size
Dequeue is O(1), but the shifted elements stay referenced, so garbage collection dominates the run time
The array has poor locality at large sizes, which makes both enqueue and dequeue linear in the capacity
rubric: Shifting n-1 elements per dequeue is O(n), giving quadratic total drain cost.
Distractors blame resizing or caching, but resizing stays amortised O(1) and shifting is the actual bottleneck.

proficient.prompt: A min-heap stored in an array uses 0-based indexing. A developer's `parent(i)` returns `i / 2` with integer division, and the heap property is violated after several inserts. What is the most likely cause?
options: For 0-based indexing the parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, so sift-up compares nodes with wrong parents and misplaces elements
Integer division truncates, so parent indexes are always too small and sift-up never executes at all
A min-heap needs children at `2i` and `2i + 1`, so the child formula is what is wrong and not the parent
Sift-up must start from the root and proceed downward, so the direction of the loop breaks the property
rubric: With 0-based arrays children are 2i+1 and 2i+2, so the parent is (i-1)/2.
Distractors misattribute the fault to truncation, 1-based child formulas or sift direction.

proficient.prompt: A depth-first search on a graph with cycles is written recursively and does not record visited nodes. It works on trees but loops forever on some graphs. What explains the difference?
options: Trees have no cycles, so no node is reached twice, whereas a cycle lets the search return to a node on its own path
Trees have fewer edges than graphs, so the recursion depth stays under the stack limit and the search finishes
Graphs have weighted edges, so DFS cannot choose which neighbour to follow first and keeps alternating
Trees are always stored as adjacency matrices, which mark visited nodes automatically during traversal
rubric: Cycles let DFS revisit nodes indefinitely without a visited set.
Distractors invoke depth limits, weights or storage format, which are unrelated to the cause.

proficient.prompt: A service stores 5 million user records in a hash table keyed by a string built from the user's signup timestamp in seconds. Insert rates are high and lookups slow down in bursts. Which findings would explain the bursts? Select all that apply.
options: Many users sign up in the same second, so identical keys or near-identical hash inputs fall into the same bucket
The hash function uses only the last few characters, so keys differing in earlier characters collide
Resizing rehashes every entry, so an insert that triggers growth takes O(n) at that moment
Hash tables lose speed when keys are strings, so every lookup compares full string lengths in O(n)
rubric: Clustered keys, weak hash functions and rehash pauses all cause bursty slowdowns.
String comparison cost depends on key length, not on table size, so it does not explain bursts.

proficient.prompt: An engineer implements LRU cache using a singly linked list plus a hash map from key to node. Gets are expected to be O(1), but profiling shows removing a node on cache hit takes time proportional to cache size. The map lookup itself is fast. What is the root cause?
options: A singly linked node has no pointer to its predecessor, so unlinking it requires scanning from the head
The hash map stores nodes by value, so each hit copies the full list before moving the node to the front
Moving a node to the front of a list is inherently O(n) in every linked list, whatever its pointers
The map must be rebuilt after each hit because list order changes the hash of every key
rubric: Removing a node in O(1) needs its predecessor, which a doubly linked list provides.
Distractors invent copying, inherent O(n) moves or rehashing, none of which applies.

proficient.prompt: You must support frequent 'insert a number' and 'remove the smallest' operations on a stream, with up to 10 million items, and never need arbitrary lookups. Criteria: lowest worst-case cost per operation and compact memory. Which structure is best?
options: A binary min-heap in an array, with O(log n) insert and remove-min and no per-node pointers
A sorted array, since remove-min is O(1) and binary search finds the insertion point quickly
A balanced BST, since it gives O(log n) for every operation and also supports arbitrary lookups
A hash table keyed by value, since inserts are O(1) and the minimum is found by hashing
rubric: A heap meets both criteria; array storage avoids pointers.
A sorted array has O(n) inserts, a BST adds pointer overhead for unneeded features, and hashing does not order keys.

proficient.prompt: A read-heavy lookup table of 50,000 fixed integer keys is built once at startup, never changes, and needs ordered range queries ('all keys between a and b'). Criteria: simplest design with fast queries. Which choice is best?
options: A sorted array with binary search for the range start, then a linear scan through the matching items
A hash table with chaining, because lookups are O(1) and range queries scan only the relevant buckets
A self-balancing tree, because it handles inserts and deletes, which this fixed data set will require
A linked list kept sorted, because traversal from the head reaches the range start in O(log n)
rubric: Static data plus range queries favours a sorted array: simple, compact, O(log n) start.
Hash tables do not keep order; balanced trees add unneeded complexity; linked lists cannot binary search.

proficient.prompt: A road network has 2 million intersections but each connects to at most 6 others. You need neighbour iteration and memory efficiency. Evaluate representations: which is the best justified?
options: An adjacency list, because memory is O(V+E) and neighbours of a node are iterated in time proportional to their count
An adjacency matrix, because edge existence is O(1) and the 4 trillion cells are acceptable for such a network
An edge list, because it supports neighbour iteration in O(1) by indexing directly into the node's edges
An adjacency matrix, because sparse graphs need the matrix to avoid pointer overhead on every edge
rubric: The graph is sparse, so adjacency lists use O(V+E) memory and iterate neighbours efficiently.
A matrix would need V^2 cells, and an unsorted edge list needs a scan to find a node's edges.

proficient.prompt: A team debates implementing a stack for an undo feature. Expected use: up to a few thousand pushes, pops only from the top, and tight latency without pauses. Which critique of the options is most sound?
options: A dynamic array is fine: amortised O(1) pushes with good locality, and the rare resize cost is small at this size
A linked list is clearly superior, because arrays can never support O(1) push and pop in any circumstance
A balanced BST is best, since stack ordering is recovered through in-order traversal in O(1) time
A queue is best, since undoing the oldest action first matches how users expect undo to behave
rubric: Dynamic arrays give amortised O(1) push/pop with locality; at a few thousand items resizes are negligible.
Distractors overstate array limits, misuse BST traversal or confuse LIFO with FIFO.

proficient.prompt: A dictionary must keep 1 million string keys and return them in sorted order on demand every few seconds, with steady inserts. Criteria: ordered iteration without a full sort each time, and O(log n) inserts. Which is best?
options: A balanced BST, since in-order traversal yields sorted keys and inserts stay O(log n)
A hash table, since sorting its keys on demand is O(n) because buckets are already in key order
A min-heap, since iterating its array front to back returns keys in sorted order
An unsorted array, since appending is O(1) and a sort at read time costs only O(n)
rubric: Balanced trees keep order and give O(log n) updates.
Hash buckets and heap arrays are not sorted, and sorting an array costs O(n log n).

proficient.prompt: You choose between a hash table and a balanced BST for an in-memory index with 20 million keys. Requirements: predictable worst-case latency per operation, and range queries over key intervals. Which statements correctly support choosing the BST? Select all that apply.
options: A balanced BST guarantees O(log n) worst-case operations, while a hash table's worst case can degrade with collisions
In-order traversal from a start key gives range results directly, which hashing cannot do
A hash table's resize can cause one insert to cost O(n), which hurts predictable latency
A BST is smaller in memory than a hash table because it avoids storing any pointers
rubric: Worst-case bounds, ordered traversal and resize pauses all favour the BST for these criteria.
BST nodes store child pointers, so the memory claim is false.

proficient.prompt: A scheduler must pick the highest-priority task each tick. Tasks arrive constantly, priorities of waiting tasks rarely change, and there are about 100,000 waiting tasks. A colleague proposes a sorted linked list so the top item is always at the head. Evaluate the proposal against throughput.
options: It is weak: each insert walks the list in O(n), whereas a binary heap does insert and extract in O(log n)
It is strong: the head gives O(1) extraction and insertion is O(1) because linked lists never shift elements
It is weak: extraction from the head of a list is O(n) because every node must be relinked to the tail
It is strong: sorted lists beat heaps for inserts because heaps need O(n) to restore order after each push
rubric: Sorted list insertion needs a linear search for position; a heap gives O(log n) insert and extract.
Distractors wrongly claim O(1) sorted insertion, O(n) head removal or O(n) heap repair.
